::: {.publication-details}
**Variational Early Fault-Tolerant Quantum Computing**

Nico Meyer, Christopher Mutschler, Dominik Seuß, Andreas Maier, Daniel D. Scherer.

*IEEE International Conference on Quantum Computing and Engineering (QCE)*, vol. 2, pp. 672–673, September 2026 (proceedings to appear).

<p class="publication-abstract">This short conference version of “Learning Logical Operations for Arbitrary Quantum Error Correction Codes” describes VarEFTQC, a method for designing noise-adapted quantum codes together with their logical gates. It demonstrates a five-qubit non-additive code with a shallow universal gate set tailored to structured depolarizing noise.</p>

:::

::: {.publication-details}
**[Learning Logical Operations for Arbitrary Quantum Error Correction Codes](https://journals.aps.org/pra/abstract/10.1103/qj2x-3l6n)**

Nico Meyer, Christopher Mutschler, Dominik Seuß, Andreas Maier, Daniel D. Scherer.

*Physical Review A* **114**, 032424, 2026.

<p class="publication-abstract">A learning-based framework finds physical implementations of logical gates directly from an encoding circuit, including for non-additive error-correcting codes. It also jointly optimizes encodings and logical operations for specific noise and gate-set requirements, with demonstrations on standard codes and an accompanying software library.</p>

:::

![](images/publication-03-figure-1.png){.publication-image .lightbox fig-alt="Schematic of noise-aware code concatenation"}

<p class="publication-figure-credit">Image credit: Figure 1, Meyer et al., QCE 2026 · © 2026 IEEE · <a href="https://ieeexplore.ieee.org/Xplorehelp/downloads/license-information/IEEE.html">reuse terms</a></p>

::: {.publication-details}
**[Learning to Concatenate Quantum Codes](https://doi.org/10.48550/arXiv.2604.14931)**

Nico Meyer, Christopher Mutschler, Dominik Seuß, Andreas Maier, Daniel D. Scherer.

*IEEE International Conference on Quantum Computing and Engineering (QCE)*, vol. 1, pp. 2838–2844, September 2026 (proceedings to appear; linked preprint).

<p class="publication-abstract">This work adapts each level of quantum-code concatenation to the effective noise left by the preceding level. Learned, small encoders handle structured noise before conventional codes take over; simulations show that this combination can reach target logical error rates with substantially fewer physical qubits.</p>

:::

::: {.publication-details}
**[Optimized Compilation of Logical Clifford Circuits](https://ieeexplore.ieee.org/document/11668561)**

Alexander Popov, Nico Meyer, Daniel D. Scherer, Guido Dietl.

*IEEE International Conference on Quantum Control, Computing, and Learning (qCCL)*, vol. 1, pp. 1–6, July 2026.

<p class="publication-abstract">Rather than compile logical Clifford circuits gate by gate, the paper examines larger circuit blocks for an error-detecting code family. It derives depth-efficient compilation patterns from small instances and reports lower simulated error rates for several circuit structures.</p>

::: {.publication-details}
**[Variational Quantum Error Correction](https://ieeexplore.ieee.org/document/11249827)**

Nico Meyer, Christopher Mutschler, Andreas Maier, Daniel D. Scherer.

*IEEE International Conference on Quantum Computing and Engineering (QCE)*, vol. 2, pp. 456–457, September 2025.

<p class="publication-abstract">This short conference version of “Learning Encodings by Maximizing State Distinguishability: Variational Quantum Error Correction” uses the distinguishability of noisy quantum states to train noise-adapted error-correcting codes. It compares the learned encodings with standard codes and includes proof-of-concept experiments on quantum hardware.</p>

::: {.publication-details}
**[Learning Encodings by Maximizing State Distinguishability: Variational Quantum Error Correction](https://iopscience.iop.org/article/10.1088/2058-9565/ae98b1)**

Nico Meyer, Christopher Mutschler, Andreas Maier, Daniel D. Scherer.

*Quantum Science and Technology* **11**(4), 045036, 2026.

<p class="publication-abstract">Maximizing the distinguishability of encoded states after noise provides a training objective for variational quantum error correction. The resulting noise-adapted codes can reduce resource demands relative to standard codes in the studied settings; proof-of-concept tests run on IBM and IQM hardware.</p>

:::

::: {.publication-details}
**[BenchQC – Scalable and modular benchmarking of industrial quantum computing applications](https://doi.org/10.48550/arXiv.2504.11204)**

Florian Geissler, Eric Stopfer, Christian Ufrecht, Nico Meyer, Daniel D. Scherer, Friedrich Wagner, Johannes M. Oberreuter, Zao Chen, Alessandro Farace, Daria Gutina, Ulrich Schwenk, Kimberly Lange, Vanessa Junk, Thomas Husslein, Marvin Erdmann, Florian Kiwit, Benjamin Decker, Greshma Shaji, Etienne Granet, Henrik Dreyer, Theodora-Augustina Dragan, Jeanette Miriam Lorenz.

*International Quantum Engineering Conference and Exhibition (QUEST-IS)*, Springer CCIS vol. 2743, pp. 207–216, December 2025 (linked preprint).

<p class="publication-abstract">BenchQC develops an application-led framework for evaluating quantum solutions to industrial use cases. Using the open-source QUARK platform, it measures the full workflow from application to hardware and compares approaches to identify where quantum computing might offer practical value.</p>

::: {.publication-details}
**[Benchmarking Quantum Reinforcement Learning](https://proceedings.mlr.press/v267/meyer25b.html)**

Nico Meyer, Christian Ufrecht, George Yammine, Georgios Kontes, Christopher Mutschler, Daniel D. Scherer.

*International Conference on Machine Learning (ICML)*, PMLR vol. 267, pp. 43934–43964, July 2025.

<p class="publication-abstract">To compare quantum and classical reinforcement learning more reliably, the paper proposes statistical measures of sample complexity and outperformance. Experiments on a configurable benchmark question some earlier quantum-advantage claims while identifying more limited settings in which advantages may remain possible.</p>

<p class="publication-abstract">The RegQPG algorithm regularizes quantum policy-gradient training using Lipschitz bounds to improve robustness and generalization. ::: {.publication-details}
**[An Empirical Comparison of Optimizers for Quantum ML with SPSA-based Gradients](https://doi.org/10.1109/QCE57702.2023.00058)**

Marco Wiedmann, Marc Hölle, Maniraman Periyasamy, Nico Meyer, Christian Ufrecht, Daniel D. Scherer, Axel Plinge, Christopher Mutschler.

*IEEE International Conference on Quantum Computing and Engineering (QCE)*, vol. 1, pp. 450–456, September 2023.

<p class="publication-abstract">This study combines the low-cost gradient estimates of SPSA with conventional gradient-based optimizers for variational quantum circuits. In regression experiments, the hybrid method converges faster and more accurately than the compared alternatives, including under sampling and hardware noise.</p>

**[Quantum Natural Policy Gradients: Towards Sample-Efficient Reinforcement Learning](https://doi.org/10.1109/QCE57702.2023.10181)**

Nico Meyer, Daniel D. Scherer, Axel Plinge, Christopher Mutschler, Michael J. Hartmann.

*IEEE International Conference on Quantum Computing and Engineering (QCE)*, vol. 2, pp. 36–41, September 2023.

<p class="publication-abstract">Quantum natural policy gradients use an efficient approximation of the quantum Fisher information matrix to train reinforcement-learning policies. The experiments report faster, more stable learning and lower sample requirements than first-order training, with an additional demonstration on a 12-qubit device.</p>

:::

*International Conference on Machine Learning (ICML)*, PMLR vol. 202, pp. 24592–24613, July 2023.

<p class="publication-abstract">The paper improves quantum policy-gradient training by optimizing how measurements of a variational quantum circuit are decoded into actions. The method performs better across several benchmarks and enables a complete training run on a five-qubit quantum device.</p>

*IEEE International Conference on Quantum Computing and Engineering (QCE)*, vol. 1, pp. 31–37, September 2022.

<p class="publication-abstract">Incremental data uploading interleaves feature-encoding gates with trainable gates so high-dimensional data can enter a quantum classifier without costly preprocessing.
